full_judgment:
"The fundamental principle of a criminal trial is that the accused shall be presumed innocent and that he is not required to adduce evidence to prove his innocence but the entire burden of proof of his guilt lies on the prosecution alone and till that time the presumption of innocence continues, whether the case is before the trial Court or at Higher forums. Again law does not require a particular number of witnesses to prove a case and conviction may be founded on the testimony of an solitary witness. But rule of prudence, if not rule of law, requires corroboration of such evidence." 

 (3) If the circumstantial evidence does not furnish conclusive proof of guilt of the accused or in other words if there be reasonable explanation of the incriminating circumstances other that the guilt of the accused he cannot be convicted merely on the ground that the circumstantial evidence provide a ground for strong suspicion against him. 

 29. Thus from the evidence on record, we find that the story of Malai going towards the bazar following deceased Siddique Ali on the date of occurrence and seen the place of occurrence by the witness has not been conclusively proved. Even if it is presumed to be true that Malai was going to the bazar following the deceased Siddique Ali and found on the way to the bazar behind the deceased Siddique Ali, his mere presence on the way to the bazar through which so many persons were passing, is not enough to hold that appellant Malai was the person who committed the murder and there is enough scope to harbour doubt about the prosecution case. In the absence of any eye witness to the murder and in the absence of the positive evidence that appellant Malai was found to have followed the deceased Siddique Ali with sharp cutting weapons in hand and in the absence of proof of any overt act on the part of the deceased it cannot be said with reasonable certainty that appellant Malai was responsible for the murder of deceased Siddique Ali. 

 30. Now let us turn to the judgment and order of conviction passed by the trial court to see what reasons have been assigned by the learned Trial Court in passing the order of conviction and sentence against the appellant. The learned Trial court appears to have made up his mind drawing adverse presumption from the fact that the appellant Malai remained absconding after the occurrence and the appellant did not go to the police station for the purpose of assisting the informant in lodging the F.I.R. Though he is related to her and he also did not attend the funeral performance of the deceased. This circumstance is so remote that it cannot be taken as a ground for holding the accused appellant guilty to the offence in the absence of direct evidence or circumstantial evidence of conclusive nature. It has been found in the case of State Vs Badsha Mollah reported in 41 DLR 11 that mere absconding after the evidence is not a proof of guilt against the accused in the absence of legal evidence. The learned trial court has not also taken into consideration the defence version of case that the deceased was a man of questionable character and the occurrence might have taken place at a different place in a different manner and by different persons. It has been found in the case of Muslimuddin and others Vs. State reported in 38 DLR. (AD) 311 (relevant 312) that if the defence put forward on behalf of the accused there is reasonable possibility of being true accused is entitled to a verdict of benefit of doubt.
